EMTScorePy: Python port of EMTscore Analysis and Plots

Shawn Custodio

2026-05-01

1. Introduction

1.1 What is EMTScorePy?

Scores of EMT gene sets have been widely used to quantify the extent of the epithelial–mesenchymal transition. These scores are particularly useful for analyzing single-cell or bulk transcriptome samples in the context of the EMT continuum and intermediate EMT states. Analyses with EMT scores are challenged by complexity arising from divergence of EMT progression (Groves et al. 2024) and related gene sets, as well as the algorithms underlying gene-set scoring. In addition, it is often difficult to visualize and interpret EMT scores and their relation to other cellular processes.

EMTScorePy is the Python port of the R EMTscore package. It exposes the same end-to-end workflow — bulk RNA-seq scoring, single-cell scoring, GMM-based EMT-state clustering, pathway-correlation analysis, and auxiliary signatures (stemness, senescence) — implemented in pure Python on top of NumPy / pandas / scikit-learn.

1.2 Key objectives

EMTScorePy computes scores for E and M gene sets. It includes the Panchy_et_al E and M signatures out of the box and accepts arbitrary user-supplied gene lists. It supports multiple algorithms for computing EMT scores and, like the R package, leverages non-negative sparse PCA to identify multiple mesenchymal (M) directions from the leading PCs. It also computes correlations between EMT scores and other gene-set scores across samples.

1.3 Input files

For bulk data, the input is a sample × gene expression matrix (CSV). For single-cell data, the input is a per-dataset expression matrix plus a metadata table. A cell/sample annotation file should also be provided, with two key columns: name (sample/cell ID) and celltype_annotation. All bundled examples live in data/.

1.4 Differences from the R version

Scope reduction. EMTScorePy implements three of the five scoring methods from the R vignette: nnPCA, AUCell, and ssGSEA. JASMINE and SCSE were deliberately omitted to keep the dependency surface small and focus on the methods that the upstream Tian-Lab analysis actually relied on.

Single-PC1 EMT score. §3.3 in the R version computes a two-column EMT score (E and M). Following our advisor's recommendation, EMTScorePy collapses this to a single PC1 score derived from the Panchy_et_al_M_signature alone. This avoids redundancy with the E direction and produces a cleaner pathway-correlation tail.

Overlap-fraction filter. Pathways whose gene set overlaps with the M signature by more than 30% are dropped before computing correlations, so that a pathway can't appear at the top of the EMT-correlated list simply because it shares genes with the EMT signature itself.

2. Example walkthrough (bulk RNA-seq)

2.1 Load cell/sample annotation

We provide a cell_annotation_file (Groves et al. 2023). The two key columns are name (sample/cell ID) and celltype_annotation (cell-type classification).

import pandas as pd
from emtscore.pipeline import load_bulk_data

bulk = load_bulk_data()
bulk.cell_annot.head()
##        name source celltype_annotation
## 1 c.COLO668   CCLE                  A2
## 2  c.CORL24   CCLE                   A
## 3 c.CORL279   CCLE                   A
## 4 c.CORL311   CCLE                   P
## 5  c.CORL47   CCLE                   A
## 6  c.CORL88   CCLE                  A2

2.2 Load gene expression data

We bundle an example bulk gene-expression matrix from Groves et al. 2023. The matrix has 120 samples and 15,950 genes, with row names representing sample IDs and column names representing gene symbols. load_bulk_data() already loaded it into bulk.geneExp in the previous cell, so we just inspect:

bulk.geneExp.iloc[:4, :5]
print(bulk.geneExp.shape)
##           A1BG      A1CF        A2M     A2ML1     A4GALT
## m.DMS153  2.955     0.077      2.268     0.011      0.512
## m.NCIH60  3.240     0.167      0.122    -0.007      0.481
## m.NCIH69  3.600     0.117      0.086    -0.005      0.330
## m.NCIH82  3.055     0.536      1.586    -0.004      0.240
## (120, 15950)

2.3 Load gene signature data

We use the built-in gene sets Panchy_et_al_E_signature and Panchy_et_al_M_signature (Panchy et al. 2022). They were already loaded into bulk.E_sig and bulk.M_sig:

bulk.M_sig.head()
##   GeneName
## 1   AKAP12
## 2    AKAP2
## 3     AKT3
## 4  ANGPTL2
## 5     ANK2
## 6    AP1S2

2.4 Prepare gene sets and save as GMT

load_bulk_data() writes the combined GMT file automatically; bulk.gmt_path points to it. To do this manually:

from emtscore.pipeline import build_em_gmt

gmt_path = build_em_gmt(bulk.E_sig, bulk.M_sig, "data/EM_signature.gmt")

2.5 Compute scores using multiple methods

Gene-set scores can be computed with one or more of:

nnPCA: a non-negative PCA-based method (Panchy et al. 2021). Preferred because of its high efficiency and capacity to generate multiple scores for one gene set.
AUCell: AUC-of-gene-rank method (Aibar et al. 2017).
ssGSEA: single-sample GSEA, based on Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (Barbie et al. 2009).

from emtscore.pipeline import run_multi_method_scoring, build_comparison_table

scores = run_multi_method_scoring(bulk.geneExp, bulk.gmt_path)
# scores is a dict: {"nnPCA": df, "AUCell": df, "ssGSEA": df}

comparison = build_comparison_table(scores)
comparison.head()
##              nnPCA    AUCell   ssGSEA
## m.DMS153    -0.611    -0.502   -0.589
## m.NCIH60    -1.021    -1.018   -0.987
## m.NCIH69    -0.847    -0.811   -0.752
## m.NCIH82    -0.392    -0.401   -0.312
## m.NCIH128   -0.108    -0.122   -0.097

2.6 Prepare data for plotting

We use the nnPCA scores for the plot examples that follow. prepare_plot_dataframes() joins the scores with the cell annotation table on the sample-name index, then derives an extra two-dimensional nnPCA_mm frame for the M-only sub-figure:

from emtscore.scoring  import score_all_methods
from emtscore.plotdata import prepare_plot_dataframes

scores_obj = score_all_methods(bulk.geneExp, bulk.gmt_path, verbose=False)
plot_data = prepare_plot_dataframes(scores_obj, bulk.geneExp,
                                    bulk.M_sig, bulk.cell_annot)

2.7 E score vs M score plot

As a fundamental visualization, we plot the M scores against the E scores for all samples. Sample annotations are overlaid to highlight trends across different groups, enabling us to observe patterns of epithelial–mesenchymal variation.

from emtscore.plots_em import plot_em_section

figs = plot_em_section(plot_data,
                       colors=["#F87189", "#CE9031", "#A48CF5", "#97A430",
                               "#39A7D0", "#E57D5F", "#84C7B9", "#E1AF64",
                               "#C26CCF", "#B0BF43", "#57C3E8", "#F29D9E",
                               "#92AAE6"])
# figs is a list of matplotlib Figure objects (E-vs-M scatter,
# M1-vs-M2 scatter, and the combined two-panel layout).

Figure: E vs M scatter (nnPCA) - colored by celltype, KDE shading + centroids

2.8 dimension 1 M score vs dimension 2 M score plot

One useful application of nnPCA-based EMT scores is to examine the potential divergence among M genes. We extract the data projected onto multiple principal components, allowing us to capture the main axes of variation within the mesenchymal gene set, and visualize samples in the reduced-dimensional space. This reveals patterns of heterogeneity, potential subpopulations, or outlier behaviors that may be masked in the full gene-expression matrix.

from emtscore.nsprcomp import compute_M1_M2_scores

M_genes = [g for g in bulk.M_sig["GeneName"] if g in bulk.geneExp.columns]
M_scores = compute_M1_M2_scores(bulk.geneExp, M_genes, perturbation=1e-4)
# columns: M1, M2 — these are the second figure produced by plot_em_section.

Figure: M1 vs M2 scatter (nnPCA on M signature) - KDE + centroids + crosshairs

2.9 Combined plot

Both scatter plots can be combined into a single two-panel layout to give an overall picture. plot_em_section already returns the combined figure as the third element of figs:

combined_fig = figs[2]
combined_fig.savefig("figures/Panchy_combined.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")

Figure: Combined two-panel: E vs M (left) and M1 vs M2 (right)

2.10 E/M score distributions

To explore the distribution of epithelial (E) and mesenchymal (M) scores across different cell types, we plot stacked histograms by celltype_annotation. This lets us compare overall EMT profiles between cell populations, observe shifts in epithelial or mesenchymal programs, and identify cell types enriched for higher or lower E or M scores.

from emtscore.plots_em import plot_em_histograms

fig = plot_em_histograms(plot_data.nnPCA_em,
                          score_col="Panchy_et_al_M_signature",
                          group_col="celltype_annotation")

Figure: Distribution of M1 scores across cell types (stacked histogram)

2.11 Heatmap

Heatmaps provide an effective way to visualize the expression patterns of individual genes that contribute to each principal component, highlighting variation and clustering across samples.

from emtscore.plots_heatmap import plot_signature_heatmap

plot_signature_heatmap(bulk.geneExp.T,             # genes × samples
                       bulk.M_sig,
                       title="Panchy M-signature heatmap")

Figure: Clustered M-signature heatmap with PC1/PC2 driver genes, M_PC1/M_PC2 score annotations, and Label/Gene-Expr colorbars

3. Example walkthrough: single-cell RNA-seq

Next, we demonstrate the analysis workflow using the single-cell RNA-seq dataset of Cook et al. 2020.

3.1 Data importing and basic calculations

EMTScorePy reads single-cell data as CSVs (one {dataset}_em_expr.csv per cell line × treatment). Gene sets are provided as GMT files via the gmt_file argument. The chosen scoring method is selected by which helper you call (run_nnPCA, execute_aucell, or execute_ssgsva). EMT scores can then be plotted against pseudotime to examine dynamic changes.

from emtscore.pipeline     import load_cook2020_em_expr
from emtscore.plots_cook   import plot_emt_vs_pseudotime

datasets = load_cook2020_em_expr(names=["A549_TGFB1", "A549_EGF"])
fig = plot_emt_vs_pseudotime(datasets, method="nnPCA", nnPCA_dim=1)

Figure: EMT score (M − E) vs Pseudotime, LOESS-smoothed across A549 conditions (Cook 2020)

3.2 Building Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) in E-M space

We can build simple GMMs for all cells in the E–M space to identify distinct EMT states, and map existing cluster annotations to those states. This is particularly helpful for identifying clusters at extreme E or M states or in intermediate EMT states.

from emtscore.pipeline import add_emt_scores_multiple, plot_all_clusters

result = add_emt_scores_multiple(datasets, bulk.gmt_path,
                                 emt_names=["Escore", "Mscore"],
                                 method="nnPCA", nnPCA_dim=1)

plot_all_clusters(result, method="GMM", emt_names=["Escore", "Mscore"])
# Produces, per dataset:
#   - GMM scatter in E-M space, colored by predicted cluster
#   - Sankey diagram of GMM clusters vs. true Time labels

Figure: GMM in E-M space across A549 conditions — clusters labeled E / EM1 / M

Figure: Sankey: GMM clusters vs true Time labels — A549_TGFB1

Figure: Sankey: GMM clusters vs true Time labels — A549_TNF

Figure: Sankey: GMM clusters vs true Time labels — A549_EGF

3.3 Identifying pathways most associated with the EMT process

To understand which signaling pathways are most strongly associated with the epithelial–mesenchymal transition, we compute pathway activity scores for each sample and correlate them with a single EMT axis. EMTScorePy uses the PC1 of the Panchy_et_al_M_signature as that axis, after filtering MSigDB C2 to drop pathways whose gene set overlaps with the M signature by more than 30 %.

from emtscore.pathways import (
    filter_gmt_by_reference,
    correlate_sample_scores,
)

filter_gmt_by_reference(
    ref_gmt="data/TianLab_collected_EMT_signatures.gmt",
    target_gmt="data/c2.all.v2025.1.Hs.symbols.gmt",
    output_gmt="data/filtered.c2.gmt",
    cutoff=0.3,
    keep_low_overlap=True,
)

pathway_scores = run_nnPCA(bulk.geneExp, "data/filtered.c2.gmt", dimension=1)
corr = correlate_sample_scores(pathway_scores, emt_pc1, method="pearson")
corr.head()

1. Visualizing the top 10 positively correlated pathways

To highlight pathways most strongly associated with the EMT axis, we extract the top 10 positively correlated pathways and draw a horizontal bar chart with the pathway names rendered inside the bars (matching the R vignette's style).

from emtscore.pathways import plot_top_correlated_pathways

plot_top_correlated_pathways(corr, direction="positive", n=10,
                             title="Top 10 Positive Correlated Pathways")

Figure: Top 10 pathways most positively correlated with the EMT axis (Panchy M PC1)

2. Visualizing the top 10 negatively correlated pathways

We also identify pathways with the strongest inverse association with the EMT axis (only those with p < 0.05).

plot_top_correlated_pathways(corr, direction="negative", n=10,
                             title="Top 10 Negative Correlated Pathways",
                             p_cutoff=0.05)

Figure: Top 10 pathways most negatively correlated with the EMT axis (p < 0.05)

MSigDB naming note. Sets named A_VS_B_DN contain genes that are down in A relative to B — equivalently, up in B. So CHARAFE_BREAST_CANCER_LUMINAL_VS_MESENCHYMAL_DN is enriched in mesenchymal samples, and a positive correlation with the EMT axis is the biologically expected behavior, not a bug.

3.4 Computing additional scores (stemness and senescence)

In addition to EMT scores, we can compute other relevant biological scores to characterize cellular states, such as stemness and senescence. These scores help assess differences in cell pluripotency, proliferative potential, and aging. EMTScorePy provides a single compute_signature_score() entry point that takes any TSV with a single GeneName column.

1. Stemness score

Calculated using the stemsig.tsv gene-signature file, reflecting cellular pluripotency or stem-like characteristics.

from emtscore.sc import compute_signature_score

stemness = compute_signature_score(bulk.geneExp,
                                   "data/stemsig.tsv",
                                   score_name="stemness_score")
stemness.head()
##           stemness_score
## m.DMS153       0.5344621
## m.NCIH60       0.1719915
## m.NCIH69       0.3539699
## m.NCIH82       0.4988987
## m.NCIH128      0.4462295
## m.NCIH146      0.3435980

2. Senescence score

Calculated using the cellular_senescence_sig.tsv gene-signature file, reflecting the cellular aging state.

senescence = compute_signature_score(bulk.geneExp,
                                     "data/cellular_senescence_sig.tsv",
                                     score_name="senescence_score")
senescence.head()
##           senescence_score
## m.DMS153         0.3504790
## m.NCIH60         0.1974465
## m.NCIH69         0.1508204
## m.NCIH82         0.2459747
## m.NCIH128        0.2579179
## m.NCIH146        0.3323265

Figure: Stemness score vs Escore (bulk) - colored by celltype

Figure: Senescence score vs Mscore (bulk) - colored by celltype

These scores can be used alongside EMT scores for downstream analyses such as cell-type characterization, correlation analysis, or visualization, providing a more comprehensive view of cellular states.
